content: Saturated fat is a type of fat composed of triglycerides that contain only saturated fatty acids. These fatty acids lack double bonds between the carbon atoms in their chains, meaning they are fully saturated with hydrogen atoms. There are various naturally occurring saturated fatty acids, differing only in the number of carbon atoms in their chains, which can range from 1 to 24. Examples of common saturated fatty acids include butyric acid (4 carbon atoms, found in butter), lauric acid (12 carbon atoms, found in breast milk, coconut oil, and palm oil), myristic acid (14 carbon atoms, found in cow milk and dairy products), palmitic acid (16 carbon atoms, found in palm oil and meat), and stearic acid (18 carbon atoms, found in meat and cocoa butter). Fats derived from natural sources, such as animals and plants, are consumed as food and contain varying proportions of saturated and unsaturated fats. Foods high in saturated fat include butter, ghee, suet, tallow, lard, coconut oil, cottonseed oil, palm kernel oil, dairy products (especially cream and cheese), meat, and certain processed foods. Saturated fats, such as those in coconut oil and cow butter, are more solid at room temperature, more stable during cooking, and have longer shelf lives compared to oils like olive oil or other liquid vegetable oils. Hydrogenation of liquid vegetable oils increases their shelf life and makes them solid at room temperature, but these are not equivalent to pure, unadulterated saturated fats. Conversely, dehydrogenation converts saturated fats into unsaturated fats. Replacing saturated fatty acids with polyunsaturated fatty acids, particularly linoleic acid, has been shown to reduce the risk of coronary heart disease. This conclusion is supported by large randomized clinical trials, which demonstrated that replacing saturated and trans fats with polyunsaturated vegetable oils lowered coronary heart disease risk. Diets high in saturated fat have been associated with an increased incidence of atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease in both animal and human studies. Numerous studies suggest that high saturated fat intake increases the risk of heart disease and stroke. Epidemiological studies have found that diets rich in saturated fatty acids, such as lauric, myristic, palmitic, and stearic acids, are linked to a higher prevalence of coronary heart disease. Controlled experimental studies have also shown that high saturated fat diets negatively affect cholesterol profiles, which are predictors of cardiovascular disease. A 2003 meta-analysis published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition concluded that diets high in saturated fat adversely affect cholesterol profiles, increasing the risk of heart attacks and other cardiovascular diseases. Randomized studies comparing control diets to Mediterranean diets (which replace saturated fats with monoand polyunsaturated fats) showed a significant reduction in the likelihood of secondary heart attacks, cardiac death, heart failure, or stroke. Epidemiological studies have identified lauric acid consumption as a predictor of heart disease, though its impact may be smaller than that of other saturated fats like myristic and palmitic acids. The World Health Organization (WHO) has classified foods rich in lauric acid as a possible contributor to coronary heart disease. Similarly, the American Heart Association (AHA) recommends reducing saturated fat intake to less than 7% of total calories, aligning with recommendations from the WHO and the FDA. These organizations agree that reducing saturated fat consumption improves health outcomes and decreases the prevalence of heart disease. The WHO has concluded that saturated fats negatively affect cholesterol profiles, predisposing individuals to heart disease, and recommends avoiding them to reduce cardiovascular disease risk. However, some studies have found conflicting results. For example, research has shown that women who consumed the most saturated fats had the least additional atherosclerotic plaque buildup in their arteries. These women also exhibited healthier balances of HDL and LDL cholesterol, as well as more favorable blood serum concentrations of triglycerides and free fatty acids. Dr. Mary Enig, a biochemist and nutritionist specializing in fats, has argued that many studies on dietary saturated fat fail to distinguish between saturated and trans fats. She also notes that all foods contain a mixture of saturated, monounsaturated, and polyunsaturated fats. Dr. Enig emphasizes that saturated fats are essential for hormone production, cellular membrane stability, organ cushioning, and energy. Biochemical signaling processes involving G-protein and other receptors rely on lauric, myristic, and palmitic fatty acids, as these receptors must be coupled with lipids to function properly. Processes like palmitoylation and myristoylation use palmitic and myristic fatty acids, respectively, for stabilization. Myristic acid has been linked to proper immune system function and tumor suppression. A deficiency in these and other saturated fatty acids can lead to age-related declines in white blood cell function, immune system dysfunction, and even cancer. Research conducted in the 1970s by Canadian scientists on rapeseed and canola oil suggested that at least 25% of dietary fat should be in the form of saturated fat. A 2004 study of 235 postmenopausal women found that higher saturated fat intake was associated with less progression of coronary atherosclerosis. Coronary angiography of 2,243 coronary artery segments revealed similar findings, with greater consumption of polyunsaturated oils being associated with greater progression of atherosclerosis. A 2007 study of 297 acute myocardial infarction (MI) cases in Portuguese men concluded that total fat intake, lauric acid, palmitic acid, and oleic acid were inversely associated with acute MI. Low intake of total fat and lauric acid from dairy products was linked to acute MI. Some prospective studies suggest that replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat is more effective in lowering coronary heart disease risk than simply reducing total fat consumption. Dr. Enig has also highlighted the nutritional benefits of saturated fats. Lauric acid, a medium-chain fatty acid, has antimicrobial properties and serves as a precursor to monolaurin, an antimicrobial lipid. Lauric acid is a key component of human milk, providing its major antimicrobial properties, and may be a conditionally essential fatty acid since it cannot be synthesized by mammals other than lactating females and must be obtained from the diet. The lipid hypothesis, which posits that saturated fats cause heart disease, forms the basis of much of the concern surrounding saturated fat consumption. However, there are additional issues, such as the historical portrayal of partially and fully hydrogenated oils as healthier alternatives to naturally occurring saturated fats. Critics, including Dr. Enig, have suggested that vested interests and big business played a role in the negative portrayal of saturated fats. Another confounding factor may be the formation of exogenous advanced glycation end products (AGEs) and oxidation products during cooking, which some studies have not adequately controlled for. It has been suggested that the harmful effects of high-fat foods may partly result from their high glycotoxin content, beyond the effects of oxidized fatty acid derivatives.
